report:
**Conclusion:** Your skepticism is justified. It is **not established that eating dark chocolate lowers stroke risk**.

Some prospective observational studies link higher *chocolate* intake with fewer strokes: a 2012 meta-analysis of five cohorts reported a relative risk of 0.81 for the highest versus lowest intake. But that is an association, not proof that chocolate caused the difference; chocolate eaters may differ in diet, activity, health, socioeconomic factors, or illness status. [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22933736/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22933736/)

Results are also inconsistent. A large Women’s Health Initiative prospective study found **no association** of chocolate intake with stroke (or coronary disease) among participants without major chronic disease. [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6862600/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6862600/)

Most importantly, these studies generally measured chocolate broadly—not dark chocolate specifically. A systematic review noted that none of its identified studies distinguished dark from milk chocolate; several included sweets and confectionery, making effects of cocoa hard to separate from sugar and fat. [https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00394-019-01914-9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00394-019-01914-9)

Cocoa flavanols plausibly improve short-term markers such as blood pressure, but Cochrane says longer trials are needed to determine whether cocoa products improve long-term cardiovascular health. [https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD008893_effect-cocoa-blood-pressure](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD008893_effect-cocoa-blood-pressure)

So: dark chocolate may contain beneficial cocoa compounds, but the claim that eating it *reduces stroke risk* overstates currently available evidence.
